extracted.subtask_short: patent obviousness and prior art analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103, including scope/content of prior art, analogous art determinations, how to assess differences between prior art and claimed invention, and how examiners must consider applicant replies and rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s Reply Requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred. A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or unsupported assertions about common knowledge will not be considered substantively adequate; Office personnel may repeat the rejection and make the next Office action final. (See MPEP §706.07(a).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Applicant’s Rebuttal Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results. Once rebuttal evidence is presented, the examiner should reconsider initial obviousness in view of the entire record, review all rejections and proposed rejections to confirm viability, and clearly communicate findings and conclusions articulating how they are supported by the facts. Follow procedures in MPEP §706.07(a); see MPEP §2145 and MPEP §716–§716.10 for affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Considerations as Evidence of Nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain objective indicia (secondary considerations) can rebut an obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of secondary considerations include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results (citing Graham v. John Deere). These types of evidence may be submitted to demonstrate that the claimed combination produced unexpected or nonroutine results, or that ordinary skill could not have combined elements by known methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Rebuttal Evidence to Show Nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may submit evidence or argument showing why the claimed subject matter would have been nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative showings include: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the functions that each element performs separately; (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Office personnel should reconsider any initial obviousness determination in view of such evidence (see In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly & Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Under 35 U.S.C. 102 May Be Used in 35 U.S.C. 103 Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is based on particular statutory categories of 102 (e.g., 102(a)(1), (a)(2), pre‑AIA 102(a),(b),(e)). Admitted prior art may be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of statutory category. Where appropriate, applicants can overcome a rejection (e.g., by swearing behind a publication under 37 CFR 1.131). See MPEP §§901, 2121–2129, 2151–2155 for detailed prior art rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive Content of the Prior Art (enabling, inoperative devices, admissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing prior art, consider substantive attributes such as whether the prior art is enabling, whether inoperative devices are available as prior art, and whether disclosures are broad or merely preferred embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2121–§2129 for case law and discussion on enabling disclosures, the treatment of inoperative devices, scope of disclosure versus preferred embodiments, and admissions in the specification. These factors affect whether a reference can support anticipation or obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of Prior Art Determined at Time Invention Was Made (Avoid Hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art must be determined as of the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers must 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made' and consider what would have commended itself to a person of ordinary skill at that time. See MPEP §2145 for discussions on rebutting applicants' hindsight arguments and cases such as W.L. Gore & Associates v. Garlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — Burden to Establish Applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to invoke pre‑AIA 103(c) bears the burden of establishing conditions that disqualify certain prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avail the benefits of pre‑AIA 103(c) the applicant must establish that subject matter used in the rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment. For joint research agreements (post‑Dec 10, 2004), the applicant must show (A) the invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date of invention; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties. See MPEP §706.02(l)(1)–(2) and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous Art Requirement for References in 103 Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: To be proper in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, a reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering the problem. See In re Bigio; KSR v. Teleflex; In re ICON Health and Fitness; In re Klein. Examiner may state their understanding of the problem to support pertinence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Must Explain Why a Reference Is Reasonably Pertinent
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on non‑same‑field references, the examiner should explain why an inventor seeking to solve the identified problem would have looked to that reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because whether a reference is reasonably pertinent often turns on how the problem is perceived, the examiner may need to articulate factual reasons why the prior art is pertinent, considering the specification and inferences reasonably drawn by a person of ordinary skill. Applicant arguments that the examiner misconstrued the problem should be fully considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight Given to Structural and Functional Similarities
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining analogy, similarities and differences in structure and function generally carry greater weight than classification or class cross‑references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office classification and cross‑references are some evidence of analogy/nonanalogy, but courts often emphasize structural and functional similarities (see In re Ellis). Examiners should evaluate structural/functional overlap when assessing whether art is reasonably pertinent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy Considerations in Specific Arts (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous art determinations may vary by technological area; cross‑field references can be analogous when they address the same problem or are within the scope of the inventor's field of endeavor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chemical arts — references on absorbing biologically active materials can be pertinent across food/preservative contexts (Ex parte Bland); mechanical — toothbrush art applied to hair brushes due to structural similarity (In re Bigio); electrical — circuits solving rate‑limiting problems can be pertinent to pacemaker design (Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers); design — prior designs are analogous if they have the same general use as the claimed design (In re Rosen; Ex parte Pappas). Examiners should apply these principles contextually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed Invention Must Be Considered As A Whole
rubrics_metrics.description: When ascertaining differences between prior art and claims, interpret claim language and consider both the invention and prior art references as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether individual differences themselves would have been obvious. See case law (Stratoflex v. Aeroquip; Schenck v. Nortron; In re Hirao). Examiners must avoid focusing solely on an isolated structural difference or limiting the analysis to a subset of claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Reduce the Invention to a 'Gist' or 'Thrust'
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to a 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement to analyze the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting consideration to a single perceived advantage or conceptual thrust may improperly ignore express claim limitations (see W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb; Jones v. Hardy; Panduit Corp.). Examiners should analyze all claim limitations rather than treating the invention as an abstract advantage or single‑word solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of Source/Cause of a Problem Is Part of the 'As a Whole' Inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery that identifies the source or cause of a problem can be part of the patentable invention even if the remedy is thereafter obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of the cause of a problem may render the subject matter unobvious as part of the invention as a whole (In re Sponnoble). However, discovery does not always lead to patentability if the solution would have been obvious from prior art that contained the same solution (In re Wiseman). Examiners should consider whether discovery of the cause changes the obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness Rationale Must Be Articulated and Supported by Fact Findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When making an obviousness rejection, Office personnel must articulate the factual findings that support the rationale relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office action should clearly communicate findings and conclusions and articulate how the conclusions are supported by the findings. MPEP §2143 and §2144–§2144.09 discuss rationales (e.g., teaching/suggestion/motivation to combine, market forces, design incentives) and provide examples for how rationales may be used to support an obviousness finding. Follow MPEP §706.07(a) when determining finality of actions.
